## Today in One Minute

- A Towards Data Science walkthrough shows how a complete beginner built a first ETL pipeline, giving lecturers a teachable end-to-end data engineering example.
- Hugging Face published an "agent glossary" defining terms like *harness* and *scaffold*, helping staff and students talk about AI agents with shared language.
- A Google Blog piece highlights how Chromebook accessibility tools combined with Gemini (including face control) are helping students with disabilities work more independently.

## What Happened

- The Towards Data Science article documents a beginner's first ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) project: pulling data from a source, cleaning it, and loading it into a destination, with the steps and decisions explained from scratch.
- Hugging Face released a short glossary clarifying the vocabulary used around AI agents, including the difference between an agent *harness* (the runtime that calls the model and tools) and a *scaffold* (the structured prompts and control flow that guide it).
- Google describes how Chromebook accessibility features, paired with Gemini, allow students to control devices with face gestures and use AI for tasks like summarising and writing, supporting more independent learning.

## Why It Matters

- ETL is a foundational skill across SoI and business analytics modules at RP. A clear beginner narrative gives lecturers a realistic case study and gives students a manageable first project rather than an intimidating data pipeline.
- AI agent terminology is currently inconsistent across vendors and articles. A shared vocabulary helps lecturers mark student work fairly and lets students read industry blogs without getting confused by overlapping terms.
- Accessibility-plus-AI is directly relevant to RP's inclusive learning goals. Lecturers can see how mainstream AI tools (Gemini) combine with built-in OS features to support diverse learners, including those who cannot easily use a keyboard or mouse.

## Try This Today

- Open the Towards Data Science ETL article and replicate one step on your Windows 11 laptop using Python in VS Code or a free tool like Power Query in Excel: extract a small CSV, clean one column, and save the result.
- Read the Hugging Face agent glossary and write a one-sentence definition of *harness* and *scaffold* in your own words. Test it by explaining the difference to a colleague or classmate in under a minute.
- Try Windows 11's built-in accessibility features (Settings > Accessibility > Eye control or Voice access) for 10 minutes, then compare what you experienced with the Chromebook face control article. Note one feature you could recommend to a student.

## Teaching Angle

- Use the beginner ETL story as a guided lab in data modules: have students follow the same Extract-Transform-Load stages with a small dataset (e.g. RP canteen menu, student survey CSV) and reflect on what was hardest.
- Run a 15-minute vocabulary clinic for staff or students on agent terms. Show the Hugging Face glossary, then ask learners to label parts of a simple agent diagram (model, harness, scaffold, tools).
- In a tutorial, demo one accessibility feature with Gemini or Copilot side-by-side, then run a short discussion: "Which of your assignments could a student with limited hand mobility complete more easily with these tools?" Link this to inclusive assessment design.

## Links

- [I Built My First ETL Pipeline as a Complete Beginner. Here's How.](https://towardsdatascience.com/i-built-my-first-etl-pipeline-as-a-complete-beginner-heres-exactly-how/)
- [Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right](https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-glossary)
- [Here's how accessibility tools and Gemini are helping students find independence](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/chromebooks/face-control/)
